_banner: commands.json -- everything that turns CANONICAL TEXT into ACTION.
vocabulary.json turns sound into text and decides nothing. This file decides,
and it is the ONLY place that does: the phrases the daemon speaks, the intents
that need a spoken confirmation, the stale things it refuses, and the registry
that routes an utterance either to a literal argv or to the coding agent.
THIS FILE EXISTS BECAUSE THE ARGUMENT AGAINST IT WAS WRONG IN ONE PLACE AND
RIGHT IN THE OTHER. jarvis.py's banner used to say there was 'no deterministic
shell routing ... left out on purpose: two places that know what build means
drift apart, and the agent is the one that can read the banner it is about to
contradict.' The drift argument is sound and is why this is ONE file rather
than a table inlined next to the state machine. The conclusion drawn from it
was not: routing everything through the agent charges ~3.5 s of fixed CLI
overhead before the model is even reached (--version 0.12 s, auth status
0.97 s, -p to first verdict 3.62 s, all measured) plus a network round trip,
to answer 'git status'. A closed set of literal argvs costs the process spawn
and nothing else, and it cannot mis-read the request, because it either
matched a pattern in this file or it did not.
So the split is by KIND, not by convenience. An `argv` entry is a fact about
this repository that a regex can decide -- which binary, which flags. A
`prompt` entry is a judgement -- why is something the default, what does the
banner say, what changed and does it matter. Anything matching NOTHING here
still goes to the agent as free text, so the registry is a fast path and never
a gate: an unknown utterance is answered, not refused.
SUBSTITUTION IS DELIBERATELY ALMOST ABSENT. An argv element may contain {repo}
or {threads} and nothing else, expanded from the daemon's own configuration.
NO TRANSCRIPT TEXT EVER REACHES AN argv. That is the whole safety argument for
letting a microphone start a process: the set of things it can run is closed,
written down here, and reviewable in a diff. A mis-heard word can pick the
wrong entry -- it cannot invent one, and it cannot add a flag. jarvis.py
REJECTS any other {token} at load time rather than passing it through, so a
typo here fails loudly at startup instead of running with a literal brace.
`prompt` entries do take {text}, the normalised utterance, because that is the
question being asked; it travels as one list element to `claude -p` and never
touches a shell.
ORDER MATTERS AND IS CHECKED, NOT TRUSTED. Patterns are tried in file order and
the first match wins, so 'run the fast tests' must precede 'run the tests'.
That is exactly the kind of ordering that rots silently as entries are added,
so every entry carries `examples` and `python3 voice/jarvis.py --selftest`
asserts that each example routes to its OWN entry. A new entry that shadows an
older one fails the self-test with both ids named.
THE DEFAULTS HERE ARE NOT THE DRIVERS' DEFAULTS, AND THAT IS THE POINT.
demonstrator/rb_high_ra bare is nx=2000, ny=1000, Ra=1e14, tf=40
(rb_high_ra.cpp:716-719): two million cells at a Rayleigh number CLAUDE.md
records as DIVERGING by t/t_ff ~ 30 with either initial condition, on an 8 GB
machine. A spoken 'run Rayleigh-Benard at high Rayleigh' must not mean that, so
the entry carries the 200x100 Ra=1e6 settings CLAUDE.md measures as usable.
Likewise static_droplet: gamma <= 20 is converged by 8000 steps, gamma = 100
reads 2.12% at 8000 against 3.21% at 32000, so the gamma-100 entry pays the
32000 steps and the plain entry stays at gamma 20 rather than quoting a
transient.
--kokkos-num-threads IS APPENDED BY HAND ON EVERY BINARY. ctest supplies it via
LBM_TEST_ARGS (CMakeLists.txt:134-143); a direct invocation without it runs
single-threaded, several times slower, with no warning.
WHAT THIS FILE DOES NOT DO. It does not parse parameters out of speech: there
is no entry that turns 'at gamma fifty' into '-gamma 50', because that would
put transcript-derived text into an argv and the grid flag is not even the same
letter across drivers (-n for static_droplet and ehd_cavity, -ny for
rb_high_ra, -h for rayleigh_benard, -d for tgv3d). Ask for a parameter this
file does not name and the agent takes it, which is the right division: it can
read the driver's own parser. It also does not background anything -- every
argv runs to completion under a wall-clock cap while the voice loop waits, so
`slow: true` exists to warn aloud first. A detached run on this Mac is
QoS-throttled to ~14% CPU, which is worse than waiting.
spoken_style: You are answering out loud through a speech synthesiser, so the reply is heard once and cannot be re-read. Answer in at most two short sentences of plain prose. No markdown, no bullet points, no code blocks, no file paths and no URLs. Do not read out long numbers: give the one figure that matters, to three significant figures. If you ran something, say whether it passed or failed first. If the request was ambiguous, say what you assumed.

phrases.gapped: The microphone stream is dropping audio, so I will not guess at that. Free the machine and try again.
phrases.not_confirmed: Not confirmed. I have dropped it.
phrases.confirm_expired: The confirmation window closed, so I dropped it. Nothing was run.
phrases.confirm_gapped: The microphone stream is dropping audio, so I will not act on a confirmation I might have mis-heard. I have dropped it.
phrases.d3q19: D3Q19 was removed from the tree in September. Nothing was run.
phrases.mic_dead: The microphone has gone silent. I am stopping, because I cannot tell a dead device from a quiet room once I am listening to zeroes.

destructive.label: delete something
destructive.why: The plain verbs above are the ones a word list thinks of; these are the ones people say. Two of them were live MIS-ROUTES rather than misses: 'blow away the build tree' matched the build entry's noun pattern and silently ran cmake --build, and 'scrap the uncommitted work' matched git_status. A destructive phrasing landing on an unrelated command is worse than one landing nowhere.  SEPARABLE PARTICLES: the contiguous form missed the way the verb is actually spoken.  'blow away the build tree' matched and 'blow it away' did not -- English separates the particle around the object, and the pronoun form is the commoner one in speech because the object was already named in the previous sentence.  Measured before the fix: 'blow it away' and 'throw it away' reached the agent as free text with no confirmation, while 'wipe it' and 'delete it' were caught.

destructive.label: change or throw away work in the tree

_destructive_is_not_the_boundary: THIS LIST IS A COURTESY FOR OBVIOUS PHRASING. IT IS NOT THE SECURITY
BOUNDARY, AND READING IT AS ONE IS THE MISTAKE THIS NOTE EXISTS TO STOP.
It matches words in the TRANSCRIPT. A user does not have to SAY a
destructive word for the agent to CHOOSE a destructive action: 'jarvis, the
build directory is stale, sort it out' contains no word any list would
carry, and the agent's reasonable response to it is to delete the build
tree. Twenty-two utterances were run through the real gate(); thirteen
reached the agent as free text with no confirmation at all, including 'get
rid of the build directory', 'throw away my changes' and 'free up some disk
space'. The entries above close the ones that can be closed, and the last
sentence of this paragraph is why that is not enough.
THE BOUNDARY IS WHAT THE CHILD IS PERMITTED TO DO: --permission-mode,
--allowedTools and --disallowedTools in jarvis.py's Agent.argv(). Until
2026-09-20 that boundary was open -- Bash(cmake *) admits `cmake -E rm -rRf`
and `cmake -E env -- <any binary>` -- so the gate really was the only thing
standing there, and it was theatre. See READ_TOOLS in jarvis.py.
One thing is still UNVERIFIED and should be checked on a machine where the
claude CLI is logged in: whether --permission-mode dontAsk DENIES a tool
that is not on the allowlist or PROCEEDS with it. If it proceeds, the
allowlist is advisory and only --disallowedTools is load-bearing.

refuse.why: Removed 2026-09-18. It was tgv3d's DEFAULT and a documented orszag_tang option, so every saved command line from before that date carries it. campaign::dispatch is [[nodiscard]] and prints NOTHING WAS RUN; refusing out loud is the difference between the user hearing 'done' and hearing why nothing ran.

commands.why: The 19 ctest entries measured under 0.1 s each in build/Testing/Temporary/CTestCostData.txt, MINUS the two that are not (osm_city 0.179 s, osm_city_fixture 0.110 s) and minus height_field_osm, which carries FIXTURES_REQUIRED and would drag the fixture in. Measured end to end at 2.71 s wall, 19/19 passed, against about 165 s for the full suite. This is the entry that makes 'did I break anything' a question worth asking out loud.

commands.say: Running the whole suite. This takes about three minutes.
commands.why: 38 tests. The cost is very uneven: layered_poiseuille 74.7 s, laplace 19.0 s, regularized 15.1 s, poiseuille 14.3 s, floating_body 11.8 s, gaussian_plume 10.9 s -- roughly 165 s serial -- while 20 of the 38 finish under 0.1 s. Hence the separate fast entry above, and `slow` so the daemon warns before going deaf for three minutes.
Answers the question actually asked after a suite run, and costs nothing when the last run was clean.

examples: run the colour gradient cross check
commands.say: Running the cross-code colour gradient check.
commands.why: tests/cross_colour drives BOTH colour-gradient operators through 320 identical randomised states and diffs all 27 populations; worst difference 0 exactly, at both precisions. It is the one place the two codebases are compared automatically, so it is worth being able to ask for by name.

counterexamples: get rid of the build directory
the build directory is stale sort it out
commands.why: Incremental, against the existing build/ whose CMakeCache already carries CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, Kokkos_ENABLE_SERIAL=ON, Kokkos_ENABLE_THREADS=ON, LBM_PRECISION=double, LBM_TEST_THREADS=4 -- verified. -j4 not -j8: the user runs solvers on this 8 GB machine and a wider build fights them for memory. The (?<!the ) is load-bearing: 'blow away the build tree' used to match the noun `build tree` and silently RUN A BUILD, which is a destructive phrasing landing on an unrelated command rather than merely being missed.

Kokkos_ENABLE_THREADS=ON is not optional: without it CMake prints 'no host-parallel backend, tests run serial' and everything runs single-threaded, several times slower and easy not to notice. This entry exists so that the flag can never be forgotten by whoever is talking.

commands.say: Running the frame check. Read the loops and regidx columns, not the clock.
commands.why: A moment index must be a compile-time constant or the 27-moment array leaves the register file -- bit-identical answers, every test passing, and a measured 47x in GPU/'s colour gradient. This script is the ONLY instrument in the tree that can see it. The spoken line repeats what to read because the wall clock is the misleading column.
The tree's plainest validation case, and the one whose x H^2 convergence is asserted to three digits. 14.3 s under ctest.
Four acceptance lines, all PASS, and it is what separates the moment operators from BGK by a measured factor of 100. 0.69 s under ctest.

examples: run the static droplet at gamma one hundred
run the static droplet at gamma 100
commands.say: Running the static droplet at density ratio one hundred. This needs thirty-two thousand steps to converge.
commands.why: THE STEP COUNT IS THE MEASUREMENT. gamma = 100 reads 2.12% at 8000 steps, 3.11% at 16000 and 3.21% at 32000, and a 1500-step ladder gave 493% -- a number that was written into three files as a property of the model before a longer run contradicted it. Quoting gamma 100 at a short step count is the mistake this entry exists to prevent.

commands.say: Running the static droplet at density ratio twenty.
commands.why: gamma <= 20 is converged by 8000 steps (0.04 points of drift out to 32000), so this is the largest ratio that can be asked for casually and still quoted. Anything higher needs the entry above or the agent.

examples: run the natural convection grid convergence
commands.say: Sweeping natural convection against de Vahl Davis.
commands.why: -conv is natural_convection's ONLY flag (natural_convection.cpp:20). It sweeps N at fixed Ra against the 1983 table: Ra = 1e5 falls monotonically -1.00, -0.39, -0.18, -0.05% at N = 32/48/64/96, order 2.4-3.4. This is the external check on the buoyancy coupling.

Ra_c converges at order 2.36 for the midway wall pair and 1.75 for the on-node pair. -marginal and -rate are the other two studies on the same binary; ask for those by name and the agent will read the parser.

commands.say: Running Rayleigh-Benard at Rayleigh ten to the six, two hundred by one hundred.
commands.why: THE BARE DEFAULTS ARE A TRAP FOR A VOICE COMMAND. rb_high_ra.cpp:716-719 is nx=2000, ny=1000, Ra=1e14, tf=40 -- two million cells at a Rayleigh number CLAUDE.md records as DIVERGING by t/t_ff ~ 30 with either IC, on an 8 GB machine. These are the settings CLAUDE.md measures as usable: Ra = 1e6 at 200x100 gives Nu_bot/Nu_top = 7.40/7.48, agreeing to 1% and to 7% of 0.14 Ra^0.29.

commands.say: Running the EHD cavity at N one twenty nine.
commands.why: The driver's own defaults (n=129, C=10, M=10, tf=30) are the sensible ones here, so these are stated rather than changed. Note the ladder at T = 5000 is UNDER-RESOLVED at every N it reaches -- Re_cell 8.5, 6.1, 3.6 against the paper's 1.6 -- so do not quote a converged Ne from this.

commands.say: Running Orszag-Tang on D2Q9 with central moments.
commands.why: N=256 rather than the driver's 512: a quarter of the cells, and this runs while the user waits. -lat is stated explicitly because orszag_tang validates -lat, -maglat and -op up front and a stale d3q19 is now a hard error.

commands.say: Running the Manchester plume at diffusivity twenty.
commands.why: -diff 20, NOT the default 5. Manchester at -diff 5 reports a stability margin of 48x against the 100x threshold and DIVERGES at t = 60 s; -diff 20 gives 192x and runs. geom/mcr exists in the tree (mcr_heights.npy + mcr_meta.json), so this entry is runnable as written.

Read-only, instant, and the single most common thing to ask a repository. Routing it to the agent would charge 3.5 s of CLI overhead plus a network round trip to run the same command. `empty_say` matters here: `git status --short` prints NOTHING when the tree is clean, and 'it printed nothing' is the wrong answer to 'what's dirty'. THE BARE \buncommitted\b IS GONE: it swallowed 'scrap the uncommitted work', i.e. a request to DESTROY that work ran a status instead. Both the contracted and the expanded forms are listed because whisper emits either -- synthesised 'jarvis what is running' came back from tiny.en as the expanded form unprompted.

examples: what am I ahead of main by
commands.empty_say: Nothing on this branch yet. It is level with main.
commands.why: Empty output is the CORRECT answer here and not a failure: the Voice branch had zero commits ahead of main when this file was written, so the first thing anyone asks returns nothing. Saying 'it printed nothing' would read as a broken command.

The user runs long solves while working -- load average 19-27 was the normal state during this file's measurements -- and 'is it still going' is a real question. uptime answers it in one short line that speaks well; ps output does not. Both "what's running" and "what is running" are listed: the registry had only the contracted form, whisper emitted the expanded one, and the command fell through to the agent -- an API round trip for something answered locally in milliseconds.

commands.confirm_label: kill every solver process running out of this build tree
commands.why: THE ONE ROUTED COMMAND THAT DESTROYS WORK, hence confirm. Note the bare word 'stop' is NOT here: jarvis.py treats a short 'stop' as the cancel word, which must stay free. TWO THINGS WERE WRONG WITH THE FIRST VERSION. The pattern was the unanchored RELATIVE fragment `build/(validation|demonstrator)/`, and pkill -f matches the full argument vector of every process this user owns -- so it also killed `vim .../build/validation/poiseuille.cpp`, a `tail -f build/demonstrator/urban.log`, an unrelated Claude Code session whose Bash tool was running a driver from that path, and a second jarvis instance's registry child. It is now anchored to THIS repo's absolute path and bounded to this uid. And pkill exits 1 when nothing matched, which is the SUCCESS case here: verdict() read that as 'stop_the_run exited with code 1 and said nothing', i.e. it reported the good outcome as a failure. rc_say fixes that. The right long-term answer is to track the PIDs this daemon started and kill those groups with reap(), which needs no pkill at all; that is not done here because a solve is usually started from the user's own terminal, not by this daemon.

examples: why is the colour gradient the default rest term
why does the phase field use central moments
commands.prompt: Answer from this repository's own banners. Find the file that implements the thing being asked about, read the banner comment at the top of it and the relevant section of CLAUDE.md, and answer with the argument and the measured number those give. If they disagree with each other, say so. The question: {text}
commands.why: A judgement, not a fact a regex can decide. The banners are the documentation in this tree and they usually already say why the obvious answer is wrong, so the instruction is to go and read one rather than to reason from training.

examples: read the banner on the colour gradient
what does the banner say about free surface
commands.prompt: Find the file being referred to, read the banner comment at the top of it, and summarise its argument in at most two spoken sentences, leading with the measured number if it has one. The request: {text}
commands.why: The banners are long and argumentative; hearing the argument and the number is the useful half.

commands.prompt: Write what we just measured into the module banner AND into doc/m3lb.tex's Known limitations, following this tree's conventions: the measured numbers rather than adjectives, an explicit statement of what the thing does NOT do, and the argument for the decision. Do not write it only into a commit message. The request: {text}
commands.confirm_label: edit a module banner and doc/m3lb.tex
commands.why: It WRITES, so it needs the spoken confirmation even though the agent also needs --allow-edits before it can act. Two gates, because a mis-heard 'write this up' that edits a banner is a silent corruption of the one thing this tree treats as documentation.

examples: add a validation case for the specular wall
commands.prompt: Write a new validation case following validation/tgv2d.cpp for shape. Include validation/Campaign.hpp rather than the solver headers directly, because the headers are not self-contained -- collision/BGK.hpp defines Macro and must precede solver/FluidSolver.hpp, so alphabetical include order fails to compile. Compare against something with a known answer (analytic, a published table, or a convergence rate) and print PASS or FAIL. Register it in the FIRST foreach of validation/CMakeLists.txt if it is a regression test, the SECOND if it is an analysis sweep. The request: {text}
commands.confirm_label: write a new source file and edit CMakeLists
commands.why: Writes a file and edits CMakeLists.txt. The prompt carries the two things that are not guessable: the include-order trap, and which of the two foreach lists a case belongs in -- the wrong list either never runs or makes ctest minutes slower.

examples: what was the last Nusselt number
commands.prompt: Find the most recent relevant run output in this repository -- results/, any run log, or the terminal scrollback if you can see it -- and report the single figure asked for, with the run's parameters, in two spoken sentences. If the run is still going or the number is from an unconverged run, say that first. The request: {text}
commands.why: Needs searching and judgement about convergence, which is exactly what a regex cannot do and the agent can.

commands.prompt: Use tools/osm_city.py to import the requested city. Resolve the place to an explicit --lat/--lon first and use those, never a place name: 'Manchester city centre, UK' geocodes today to a point 1,459 m from where the same string landed in July, which is 73% of a 2 km side. Use --fallback type for new work, not the default flat, and say which was used. The request: {text}
commands.why: Needs a coordinate lookup and a judgement call on the fallback model, so it is not a literal argv. The two traps are stated because both silently produce a plausible raster.
